focus: Exodus 34 answers Moses’ plea as the LORD calls him back up the mountain with new tablets, passes before him, and proclaims His name as merciful and gracious, forgiving yet just. The LORD renews the covenant with commands for exclusive worship and Israel’s appointed feasts, the words are written again, and Moses comes down with his face shining from speaking with Him.

sections.title: Moses Cuts New Tablets and Goes Up Sinai
sections.summary: The LORD tells Moses to cut two tablets of stone like the first ones, on which He will write the words that were on the tablets Moses broke. Moses rises early and goes up Mount Sinai alone, carrying the two tablets.

sections.title: The LORD Proclaims His Name
sections.summary: The LORD descends in the cloud and proclaims, “The LORD, the LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abounding in goodness and truth” (Exodus 34:6), forgiving sin yet by no means clearing the guilty. Moses bows and worships and asks the LORD to go among His stiff-necked people, pardon their sin, and take them as His inheritance.

sections.title: The LORD Renews the Covenant and Forbids Rival Worship
sections.summary: The LORD declares, “Behold, I make a covenant” (Exodus 34:10), and promises to do marvels and drive out the nations. Israel must make no covenant with the land’s inhabitants, must tear down their altars, and must make no molded gods, “for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (Exodus 34:14).

sections.title: The Feasts, the Firstborn, and the Sabbath Renewed
sections.summary: The LORD renews the commands for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the redemption of the firstborn, weekly rest even in plowing and harvest, and the Feasts of Weeks and Ingathering. All Israel’s men are to appear before Him three times a year, with the firstfruits brought to His house.

sections.title: The Words of the Covenant Are Written Again
sections.summary: The LORD tells Moses, “Write these words” (Exodus 34:27), because according to them He has made a covenant with Moses and Israel. Moses stays with the LORD forty days and forty nights without bread or water, and the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments, are written on the tablets.

sections.title: Moses’ Face Shines and He Veils It
sections.summary: Moses comes down with the tablets, not knowing that the skin of his face shone because he had talked with the LORD, and Aaron and the people are afraid to come near him. He gives them all the LORD’s commandments and then veils his face, removing the veil whenever he goes in to speak with the LORD.

1.brief: The LORD tells Moses, “Cut two tablets of stone like the first ones,” and He will write on them the words that were on the tablets Moses broke. God offers to renew the broken covenant.
1.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘Cut two tablets of stone like the first ones,”

God tells Moses to “cut two tablets” to replace the ones he broke (32:19). This time Moses prepares the stone, but God will write.

“and I will write on these tablets the words that were on the first tablets which you broke.”

God Himself “will write” the same words. God offers to renew the broken covenant.

2.brief: Moses is to be ready in the morning and present himself to God on the top of Mount Sinai. Moses is summoned to meet God again.
2.explain:
“So be ready in the morning, and come up in the morning to Mount Sinai, and present yourself to Me there on the top of the mountain.”

Moses is to “present yourself to Me,” standing ready before God at the summit. Moses is summoned to meet God again.

3.brief: No one may come up with Moses or be seen anywhere on the mountain, and no flocks or herds may graze before it. The mountain is again set apart for God’s presence.
3.explain:
“And no man shall come up with you, and let no man be seen throughout all the mountain;”

No one may come with him or be seen on the mountain.

“let neither flocks nor herds feed before that mountain.”

Even animals must stay away. The mountain is again set apart for God’s presence (19:12–13).

4.brief: Moses cuts two tablets like the first, rises early, and goes up Mount Sinai as the LORD commanded, carrying the tablets. Moses obeys promptly.
4.explain:
“So he cut two tablets of stone like the first ones.”

Moses prepares the tablets.

“Then Moses rose early in the morning and went up Mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him; and he took in his hand the two tablets of stone.”

He “rose early” and went up “as the LORD had commanded.” Moses obeys promptly.

5.brief: The LORD descends in the cloud, stands with Moses there, and proclaims the name of the LORD. God keeps His promise from Exodus 33:19.
5.explain:
“Now the LORD descended in the cloud and stood with him there,”

God “descended in the cloud” and “stood with him.” God comes down to meet Moses personally.

“and proclaimed the name of the LORD.”

God keeps His promise from 33:19. He reveals who He is.

6.brief: The LORD passes before him and proclaims, “The LORD, the LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abounding in goodness and truth.” God reveals His character, beginning with His mercy and faithfulness.
6.explain:
“And the LORD passed before him and proclaimed,”

As God passes by, He proclaims His name and character. This is the glory Moses asked to see (33:18).

“The LORD, the LORD God,”

God repeats His covenant name twice.

“merciful and gracious, longsuffering,”

He is “merciful,” tender like a mother’s love. He is “gracious,” giving undeserved favor. He is “longsuffering,” slow to anger, patient with sinners.

“and abounding in goodness and truth,”

The Hebrew words are chesed and emet, steadfast covenant love and faithfulness. God reveals His character, beginning with His mercy and faithfulness, right after Israel’s great sin.
6.notes: This self-description is echoed again and again in Scripture (Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 86:15; 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2).

7.brief: God keeps mercy for thousands and forgives iniquity, transgression, and sin, yet is “by no means clearing the guilty,” visiting iniquity to the third and fourth generation. God’s mercy and justice stand together in His own description of Himself.
7.explain:
“keeping mercy for thousands,”

God keeps “mercy for thousands,” reaching thousands of people or generations.

“forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin,”

He forgives every kind of sin: “iniquity,” crookedness; “transgression,” rebellion; and “sin,” missing the mark.

“by no means clearing the guilty,”

Yet mercy is not the whole picture. God does not pretend sin is not sin. His mercy does not cancel His justice. Romans 3:25–26 shows how both meet at the cross, where God is just and the justifier of the one who believes in Jesus.

“visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and the children’s children to the third and the fourth generation.”

The consequences of sin can reach “the third and the fourth generation.” Children often see, absorb, and practice their parents’ sins and values. The consequences continue where children continue in those ways (compare 20:5, “those who hate Me”). Each person still answers for his own sin (Ezekiel 18:20). God’s mercy and justice stand together in His own description of Himself.

8.brief: “So Moses made haste and bowed his head toward the earth, and worshiped.” Moses responds to God’s revelation with immediate worship.
8.explain:
“So Moses made haste and bowed his head toward the earth, and worshiped.”

Moses responds at once. He “made haste” and “worshiped.” Moses responds to God’s revelation with immediate worship.

9.brief: Moses asks the Lord to go among them, though they are stiff-necked, to pardon their sin, and to “take us as Your inheritance.” Moses pleads on the basis of the God who has just revealed His mercy.
9.explain:
“Then he said, ‘If now I have found grace in Your sight, O Lord, let my Lord, I pray, go among us,”

Moses asks God to “go among us.” God had already promised His presence (33:14, 17). Moses asks again, now on the basis of the character God has just revealed.

“even though we are a stiff-necked people;”

Moses admits the truth. They are “stiff-necked,” the very reason God gave for not going among them (33:3). Moses now gives it as the reason they need Him to go.

“and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us as Your inheritance.”

Moses includes himself: “our iniquity.” He asks God to “take us as Your inheritance,” to claim Israel as His own possession. Moses pleads on the basis of the God who has just revealed His mercy.

10.brief: God says, “Behold, I make a covenant,” and promises marvels never done in all the earth, so that all the people will see the LORD’s awesome work. God answers Moses by renewing His covenant.
10.explain:
“And He said: ‘Behold, I make a covenant.”

God answers by renewing His “covenant.”

“Before all your people I will do marvels such as have not been done in all the earth, nor in any nation;”

God promises “marvels,” wonders unlike anything done anywhere.

“and all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the LORD. For it is an awesome thing that I will do with you.”

The nations will see “the work of the LORD.” It will be “an awesome thing,” inspiring reverent fear. God answers Moses by renewing His covenant.

11.brief: Israel is to observe what God commands, and He will drive out the peoples of the land. The renewed covenant again joins God’s promise with Israel’s obedience.
11.explain:
“Observe what I command you this day.”

Israel’s part is to “observe” what God commands.

“Behold, I am driving out from before you the Amorite and the Canaanite and the Hittite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite.”

God’s part is to drive out the nations. The renewed covenant again joins God’s promise with Israel’s obedience.

12.brief: Israel must not make a covenant with the land’s inhabitants, lest it become a snare among them. Such a covenant could draw Israel into idolatry, the same danger seen at the calf.
12.explain:
“Take heed to yourself, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land where you are going,”

Israel must not make treaties with the people of Canaan.

“lest it be a snare in your midst.”

Such a covenant would be “a snare,” a trap leading to idolatry. The danger seen at the calf would return.

13.brief: Israel must destroy their altars, break their sacred pillars, and cut down their wooden images. Idolatry must be removed entirely.
13.explain:
“But you shall destroy their altars, break their sacred pillars, and cut down their wooden images”

Israel must destroy the places and objects of pagan worship. “Wooden images” were poles associated with the goddess Asherah. Idolatry must be removed entirely.

14.brief: Israel must worship no other god, “for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.” God’s jealousy is His faithful love claiming His people wholly for Himself.
14.explain:
“(for you shall worship no other god,”

The heart of the covenant is exclusive worship.

“for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God),”

God’s “name is Jealous.” His jealousy is not insecurity or envy. It is the faithful love of a husband who will not share his wife with another. Because God is wholly good, He wants what is best for His people, and nothing is better for them than Himself. His jealousy flows from His love.

15.brief: Israel must not make a covenant with the inhabitants, lest they be drawn into the nations’ idolatry and eat their sacrifices. Compromise with the nations leads to spiritual unfaithfulness.
15.explain:
“lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they play the harlot with their gods and make sacrifice to their gods,”

Idolatry is called playing “the harlot.” Turning to other gods is spiritual adultery against God, Israel’s husband.

“and one of them invites you and you eat of his sacrifice,”

A friendly invitation to a pagan feast would draw Israel into idol worship. Compromise with the nations leads to spiritual unfaithfulness.
15.notes: Numbers 25:1–3 records Israel doing exactly this at Baal of Peor.

16.brief: Israel must not take the nations’ daughters for their sons, lest they lead their sons into idolatry. Intermarriage with idolaters would draw Israel’s families away from God.
16.explain:
“and you take of his daughters for your sons,”

Intermarriage with idolaters would bring their gods into Israel’s homes.

“and his daughters play the harlot with their gods and make your sons play the harlot with their gods.”

Their wives would lead Israel’s sons into idolatry. The concern is religious, not ethnic. Solomon’s foreign wives later turned his heart to other gods (1 Kings 11:1–8).

17.brief: “You shall make no molded gods for yourselves.” The command directly answers the sin of the golden calf.
17.explain:
“You shall make no molded gods for yourselves.”

The command directly answers the sin of the “molded” calf (32:4).

18.brief: Israel must keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days in the month Abib, when they came out of Egypt. The renewed covenant restores the remembrance of the exodus.
18.explain:
“The Feast of Unleavened Bread you shall keep.”

The renewed covenant restores the feasts (23:14–17).

“Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, in the appointed time of the month of Abib; for in the month of Abib you came out from Egypt.”

The feast remembers the exodus.

19.brief: Everything that first opens the womb belongs to God, including the firstborn males of the livestock. God’s claim on the firstborn is renewed.
19.explain:
“All that open the womb are Mine, and every male firstborn among your livestock, whether ox or sheep.”

God’s claim on the firstborn is renewed (13:2, 12).

20.brief: The firstborn donkey is redeemed with a lamb, every firstborn son is redeemed, and “none shall appear before Me empty-handed.” The redemption of the firstborn and worship with offerings continue.
20.explain:
“But the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb. And if you will not redeem him, then you shall break his neck.”

The rule about donkeys is repeated (13:13).

“All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem.”

Every firstborn son is redeemed.

“And none shall appear before Me empty-handed.”

Worshipers must bring an offering (23:15).

21.brief: Israel must work six days and rest on the seventh, even in plowing time and harvest. The Sabbath must be kept even in the busiest seasons.
21.explain:
“Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest;”

The Sabbath is renewed.

“in plowing time and in harvest you shall rest.”

Even in the busiest seasons, “in plowing time and in harvest,” Israel must rest. Trusting God with their crops would be tested most when there was the most to do.

22.brief: Israel must keep the Feast of Weeks with the firstfruits of the wheat harvest and the Feast of Ingathering at year’s end. The harvest feasts are renewed.
22.explain:
“And you shall observe the Feast of Weeks, of the firstfruits of wheat harvest,”

“The Feast of Weeks” is the Feast of Harvest (23:16), seven weeks after Passover.

“and the Feast of Ingathering at the year’s end.”

“The Feast of Ingathering” comes at harvest’s end in autumn.

23.brief: Three times a year all Israel’s men must appear before the Lord, the LORD God of Israel. Regular gathering before God is restored.
23.explain:
“Three times in the year all your men shall appear before the Lord, the LORD God of Israel.”

All men must appear before God three times a year (23:17).

24.brief: God will cast out the nations and enlarge Israel’s borders, and no one will covet their land while they go up to appear before Him. God protects His people’s land when they leave it to worship.
24.explain:
“For I will cast out the nations before you and enlarge your borders;”

God promises to drive out the nations and enlarge Israel’s land.

“neither will any man covet your land when you go up to appear before the LORD your God three times in the year.”

When the men leave their farms to worship, God will protect their land. No enemy will even desire it. God protects His people’s land when they leave it to worship Him.

25.brief: Israel must not offer the blood of God’s sacrifice with leaven, and the Passover sacrifice must not remain until morning. The sacrifices must be offered as God directs.
25.explain:
“You shall not offer the blood of My sacrifice with leaven,”

No leaven may be offered with the sacrifice’s blood (23:18).

“nor shall the sacrifice of the Feast of the Passover be left until morning.”

The Passover sacrifice may not be left until morning. Exodus 12:10 adds that anything remaining until morning is to be burned with fire.

26.brief: Israel must bring the first of their firstfruits to God’s house and must not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk. Two commands first given in Exodus 23:19 are repeated in the covenant renewal.
26.explain:
“The first of the firstfruits of your land you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God.”

The best of the first harvest goes to God.

“You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.”

This command is repeated from 23:19. The Verse Explanation at 23:19 gives the three reasons for it.

27.brief: The LORD tells Moses, “Write these words,” for according to them He has made a covenant with Moses and Israel. The renewed covenant is written down.
27.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Write these words,”

God tells Moses to “write” the words He has spoken.

“for according to the tenor of these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.”

Moses and the people are both included. The renewed covenant is written down.

28.brief: Moses stays with the LORD forty days and forty nights without eating or drinking, and the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments, are written on the tablets. The covenant is restored in written form after a second long meeting with God.
28.explain:
“So he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water.”

Moses spends another “forty days and forty nights” with God, without food or water. God sustains him.

“And He wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments.”

“He wrote” most naturally refers to God, as promised in 34:1. The tablets bear “the Ten Commandments,” literally the ten words. The covenant is restored in written form after a second long meeting with God.
28.notes: Deuteronomy 10:1–4 confirms that the LORD wrote the Ten Commandments on the second tablets.

29.brief: Moses comes down with the two tablets, not knowing that the skin of his face shone because he had talked with God. Moses carries visible evidence of his time in God’s presence.
29.explain:
“Now it was so, when Moses came down from Mount Sinai (and the two tablets of the Testimony were in Moses’ hand when he came down from the mountain),”

Moses comes down with the new tablets.

“that Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone while he talked with Him.”

Moses “did not know” that his face was shining. The glory came from talking with God. Moses carries visible evidence of his time in God’s presence.
29.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “shone” comes from the same root as the noun for a horn. Here it describes rays of light. The Latin Vulgate rendered it “horned,” which led to medieval art showing Moses with horns.

30.brief: When Aaron and the people see Moses’ shining face, they are afraid to come near him. The glory reflected on Moses unsettles the people.
30.explain:
“So when Aaron and all the children of Israel saw Moses, behold, the skin of his face shone,”

Aaron and the people see the glow.

“and they were afraid to come near him.”

Even reflected glory unsettles sinful people.

31.brief: Moses calls to them, and Aaron and the rulers return to him, and Moses talks with them. Moses draws the people back to hear him.
31.explain:
“Then Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the rulers of the congregation returned to him; and Moses talked with them.”

Moses calls them back. Aaron and the leaders return and listen. Moses draws the people back to hear him.

32.brief: Afterward all the people come near, and Moses gives them all the commandments the LORD spoke on Mount Sinai. Moses delivers God’s word to the whole people.
32.explain:
“Afterward all the children of Israel came near, and he gave them as commandments all that the LORD had spoken with him on Mount Sinai.”

All the people come near, and Moses gives them God’s “commandments.” Moses delivers God’s word to the whole people.

33.brief: When Moses finishes speaking, he puts a veil on his face. The veil covers the shining after Moses has delivered God’s message.
33.explain:
“And when Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil on his face.”

After speaking, Moses puts on “a veil.” The veil covers the shining once he has delivered God’s message.

34.brief: Whenever Moses goes in before the LORD, he removes the veil until he comes out and tells the people what he has been commanded. Moses speaks with God unveiled.
34.explain:
“But whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with Him, he would take the veil off until he came out;”

Before God, Moses removes the veil. Moses speaks with God unveiled.

“and he would come out and speak to the children of Israel whatever he had been commanded.”

He then tells the people what God commanded.

35.brief: Whenever the people see Moses’ shining face, he puts the veil back on until he goes in to speak with God again. The pattern continues, and 2 Corinthians 3:7–18 later develops the meaning of the veil.
35.explain:
“And whenever the children of Israel saw the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses’ face shone,”

The people saw that his face shone each time.

“then Moses would put the veil on his face again, until he went in to speak with Him.”

Moses would cover his face again until his next meeting with God. Exodus describes the pattern but does not explain all of Moses’ reasons for the veil. Exodus reports the shining and the veil. Paul later uses them in 2 Corinthians 3:7–18 to describe new covenant life in Christ. He says Moses veiled his face so that Israel could not look steadily at the end of the fading glory (2 Corinthians 3:13). He says a veil still lies on the heart when Moses is read, but “when one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16). Then believers, “with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18).
